body.statement:
Let \(\mathcal W\) be a finite observed vector containing a treatment subvector \(\mathcal X\) and a single finite outcome vertex \(\mathcal Y\).  Let \(\mathbf Q_0\) and \(\mathbf Q_1\) be finite SCMs with positive rational local tables such that \(P_0(\mathcal W=w)=P_1(\mathcal W=w)\) for every observed cell \(w\), but, for some assignments \(x,y\),
\[
 P_0(\mathcal Y=y\mid\operatorname{do}(\mathcal X=x))
 \ne
 P_1(\mathcal Y=y\mid\operatorname{do}(\mathcal X=x)).
\]
Append binary vertices \(\mathcal C\) and \(\mathcal S\), driven by private exogenous variables independent of the old exogenous variables, and use the same new kernels in both SCMs.  For rational numbers \(g_u(c)\) satisfying \(g_u(c)>0\) and \(\sum_{c=0}^1g_u(c)=1\) for every outcome value \(u\), choose rational \(\lambda_c\) such that
\[
 0<\lambda_c<\min_u g_u(c),
 \qquad c\in\{0,1\},
 \qquad
 \Lambda:=\lambda_0+\lambda_1,
\]
and set
\[
 P(\mathcal C=c\mid\mathcal Y=u)=g_u(c),
 \qquad
 P(\mathcal S=1\mid\mathcal Y=u,\mathcal C=c)
   =\frac{\lambda_c}{g_u(c)}.
\]
Then the two extended SCMs are positive and rational and, for \(j\in\{0,1\}\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
 P_j(\mathcal W=w,\mathcal C=c,\mathcal S=1)
   &=P_j(\mathcal W=w)\lambda_c,\\
 P_j(\mathcal S=1\mid\operatorname{do}(\mathcal X=x))
   &=\Lambda,\\
 P_j(\mathcal C=c\mid\operatorname{do}(\mathcal X=x),\mathcal S=1)
   &=\frac{\lambda_c}{\Lambda},\\
 P_j(\mathcal Y=y,\mathcal C=c\mid
       \operatorname{do}(\mathcal X=x),\mathcal S=1)
   &=P_j(\mathcal Y=y\mid\operatorname{do}(\mathcal X=x))
     \frac{\lambda_c}{\Lambda}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Consequently the full selected observational laws and every positive conditioning denominator agree, whereas the displayed selected joint numerators and conditional causal effects disagree.  Graph membership has the following conditional form only: if the two base SCMs have a common represented graph \(\mathcal H\), if \(g_u(\cdot)\) is nonconstant in \(u\), and if \(\lambda_c/g_u(c)\) is nonconstant in \(c\) for at least one fixed \(u\), then every proposed parent is active and both extensions have the common represented graph obtained from \(\mathcal H\) by adjoining \(\mathcal Y\to\mathcal C\), \(\mathcal Y\to\mathcal S\), and \(\mathcal C\to\mathcal S\).
body.proof_tex:
Fix \(j\in\{0,1\}\). By the strict inequalities imposed on \(\lambda_c\) and the positivity of \(g_u(c)\),
\[
 0<\frac{\lambda_c}{g_u(c)}<1
 \quad\text{and}\quad
 0<1-\frac{\lambda_c}{g_u(c)}<1                         \tag{1}
\]
for every \(u\) and \(c\). Thus the displayed kernel for \(\mathcal S\), including its complementary probability for \(\mathcal S=0\), is strictly positive. The kernel for \(\mathcal C\) is strictly positive by hypothesis. All of its entries, and all entries of the \(\mathcal S\)-kernel, are rational. Since the base SCMs have finitely many states and positive rational local tables, adjoining these two binary kernels gives finite positive rational SCMs. Moreover, for any fixed \(u\), the normalization of \(g_u\) and the strict bounds on \(\lambda_c\) give
\[
 0<\Lambda=\lambda_0+\lambda_1
 <g_u(0)+g_u(1)=1.                                      \tag{2}
\]
In particular, every division by \(\Lambda\) below is legitimate.

Appending child vertices changes no old structural equation, and their private exogenous variables are independent of all old exogenous variables. Hence the marginal law of \(\mathcal W\) remains \(P_j\). If the \(\mathcal Y\)-component of \(w\) is \(u\), the SCM factorization, the common \(\mathcal C\)-kernel, and the common \(\mathcal S\)-kernel yield
\[
\begin{aligned}
 P_j(\mathcal W=w,\mathcal C=c,\mathcal S=1)
 &=P_j(\mathcal W=w)
   P(\mathcal C=c\mid\mathcal Y=u)
   P(\mathcal S=1\mid\mathcal Y=u,\mathcal C=c)\\
 &=P_j(\mathcal W=w)g_u(c)\frac{\lambda_c}{g_u(c)}\\
 &=P_j(\mathcal W=w)\lambda_c.                           \tag{3}
\end{aligned}
\]
The cancellation in the last equality is valid because \(g_u(c)>0\). Summing (3) over the finitely many \(w\) and over \(c\in\{0,1\}\) gives
\[
 P_j(\mathcal S=1)=\sum_wP_j(\mathcal W=w)
                    \sum_{c=0}^1\lambda_c
                  =\Lambda.                              \tag{4}
\]
Equations (2)--(4) therefore imply
\[
 P_j(\mathcal W=w,\mathcal C=c\mid\mathcal S=1)
 =P_j(\mathcal W=w)\frac{\lambda_c}{\Lambda}.            \tag{5}
\]
The observational-equality premise says that the right-hand side of (5) is the same for \(j=0\) and \(j=1\). Thus the two full selected observational laws agree cell by cell.

Under \(\operatorname{do}(\mathcal X=x)\), SCM modularity replaces only the structural equations for \(\mathcal X\); it leaves both appended child kernels unchanged. Marginalizing the interventional analogue of (3) over the finitely many old coordinates other than \(\mathcal Y\) gives, for every outcome value \(u\),
\[
 P_j(\mathcal Y=u,\mathcal C=c,\mathcal S=1
      \mid\operatorname{do}(\mathcal X=x))
 =P_j(\mathcal Y=u\mid\operatorname{do}(\mathcal X=x))
  \lambda_c.                                             \tag{6}
\]
Write \(p_j^x(u)=P_j(\mathcal Y=u\mid\operatorname{do}(\mathcal X=x))\). Since \(\sum_u p_j^x(u)=1\), summing (6) first over \(u,c\) and then only over \(u\) proves, respectively,
\[
\begin{aligned}
 P_j(\mathcal S=1\mid\operatorname{do}(\mathcal X=x))
   &=\sum_u p_j^x(u)\sum_{c=0}^1\lambda_c=\Lambda,\\
 P_j(\mathcal C=c,\mathcal S=1
      \mid\operatorname{do}(\mathcal X=x))
   &=\sum_u p_j^x(u)\lambda_c=\lambda_c.                 \tag{7}
\end{aligned}
\]
Dividing the second line of (7) by the first, using \(\Lambda>0\), yields the common positive conditioning denominator
\[
 D_j(c;x):=P_j(\mathcal C=c\mid
       \operatorname{do}(\mathcal X=x),\mathcal S=1)
 =\frac{\lambda_c}{\Lambda}>0.                           \tag{8}
\]
Dividing (6) at \(u=y\) by the first line of (7) gives the selected joint numerator
\[
 N_j(y,c;x):=P_j(\mathcal Y=y,\mathcal C=c\mid
       \operatorname{do}(\mathcal X=x),\mathcal S=1)
 =p_j^x(y)\frac{\lambda_c}{\Lambda}.                     \tag{9}
\]
The interventional-inequality premise gives \(p_0^x(y)\ne p_1^x(y)\). Since \(\lambda_c/\Lambda>0\), equation (9) implies \(N_0(y,c;x)\ne N_1(y,c;x)\), while (8) gives \(D_0(c;x)=D_1(c;x)\). Finally, division of (9) by (8), again justified by its strict positivity, gives
\[
 P_j(\mathcal Y=y\mid\operatorname{do}(\mathcal X=x),
       \mathcal C=c,\mathcal S=1)
 =p_j^x(y).                                               \tag{10}
\]
Thus the selected conditional causal effects differ, even though the full selected observational laws and conditioning denominators coincide.

It remains to verify the conditional graph and support claims. Under the common-graph hypothesis, the two base graphs both equal \(\mathcal H\). The independent private exogenous variables introduce no latent common cause involving an old vertex, and the two new kernels name no old parent other than \(\mathcal Y\); consequently no edge other than the three displayed arrows is added. Nonconstancy of \(g_u(\cdot)\) in \(u\) makes \(\mathcal Y\) an active parent of \(\mathcal C\). It also supplies values \(u,u'\) and a value \(c\) for which \(g_u(c)\ne g_{u'}(c)\); because \(\lambda_c>0\),
\[
 \frac{\lambda_c}{g_u(c)}
 \ne
 \frac{\lambda_c}{g_{u'}(c)},                            \tag{11}
\]
so \(\mathcal Y\) is an active parent of \(\mathcal S\). The separate hypothesis that \(\lambda_c/g_u(c)\) is nonconstant in \(c\) for some fixed \(u\) makes \(\mathcal C\) an active parent of \(\mathcal S\). Hence both extensions have the common represented graph \(\mathcal H^+\) claimed in the statement.

If every endogenous variable in each base SCM is binary, the old variables remain binary and the two appended variables are binary by construction. Together with the positive rational table conclusion and the common represented graph just proved, this places the extensions in \(\mathfrak M_{\mathrm{rat,bin}}^+(\mathcal H^+)\). Without the binary-base premise, the same argument still places the finite positive rational extensions in \(\mathfrak M_d^+(\mathcal H^+)\) under the graph hypotheses, but it does not alter or encode any nonbinary base coordinate. Therefore it does not, by itself, produce a binary certificate pair \(\Gamma\).
body.justification: The lift converts an ordinary positive rational causal witness into a denominator-locked selected conditional witness by a constructive common child and selection mechanism.
body.gap: An ordinary hedge pair need not preserve a selected conditioning denominator, so an explicit equalizing construction is required.
body.consumer: The informative table proposition instantiates this lift, and future graphical synthesis may use it whenever a common represented base witness is available.
